title: Stay Under a Million
statement: For a positive integer $n$, call a subset $S$ of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, which may be empty, closed if both of the following hold: for every positive integer $k$ with $2k \le n$, we have $k \in S$ if and only if $2k \in S$; and for every positive integer $k$ with $3k \le n$, we have $k \in S$ if and only if $3k \in S$. What is the largest positive integer $n$ for which the number of closed subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ is at most $1000000$?
hints: Take $n$ large and suppose $1 \in S$. Which other numbers are then forced into $S$? Which numbers are never affected by this choice, however large $n$ is?

Use prime factorisation to write each integer as $m \cdot 2^a \cdot 3^b$, where $m$ is coprime to $6$. Multiplying or dividing by $2$ or $3$ doesn't change $m$, so try grouping the numbers up to $n$ according to their value of $m$.

Numbers with the same $m$ must all be in $S$ or all be out of $S$, and different values of $m$ can be chosen independently. So the number of closed subsets is $2^c$, where $c$ is the number of integers from $1$ to $n$ coprime to $6$. Since $2^{19} \le 1000000 < 2^{20}$, we need $c \le 19$. It remains to list the integers coprime to $6$ in order and see where the count passes $19$.
solution: Every positive integer can be written uniquely as $m \cdot 2^a \cdot 3^b$, where $a, b \ge 0$ and $m$ is coprime to $6$. Call $m$ the core of the number. Fix $n$, and group the numbers in $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ into classes, where two numbers are in the same class exactly when they have the same core. Each class contains exactly one integer coprime to $6$, namely its core $m$, because $m$ divides every number in the class and so $m \le n$. Hence the number of classes is $c$, the number of integers from $1$ to $n$ coprime to $6$. A closed set must contain all or none of each class. To see this, take $x = m \cdot 2^a \cdot 3^b \le n$ and consider the chain $m,\ 3m,\ \dots,\ 3^b m,\ 2 \cdot 3^b m,\ \dots,\ 2^a \cdot 3^b m = x$. Every term is at most $x$, so at most $n$, and each term is $2$ or $3$ times the previous one. The conditions therefore force each term to have the same status as the previous one, so $x \in S$ exactly when $m \in S$. Conversely, any union of classes is closed. Each condition compares $k$ with $2k$ or with $3k$, and these have the same core, so they lie in the same class and have the same status. Thus closed sets correspond exactly to free choices of which classes to include, and there are $2^c$ of them. Now $2^{19} = 524288 \le 1000000$ and $2^{20} = 1048576 > 1000000$, so we need exactly $c \le 19$. As $n$ increases, $c$ never decreases, so the required $n$ is the one just before the $20$th integer coprime to $6$. The integers coprime to $6$ are those congruent to $1$ or $5$ modulo $6$, namely $$1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 25, 29, 31, 35, 37, 41, 43, 47, 49, 53, 55, 59, \dots$$ and the $20$th of these is $59$. So $n = 58$ has $c = 19$, which gives $524288$ closed subsets, while every $n \ge 59$ has $c \ge 20$, which gives more than $1000000$. The answer is $58$. Why this works. prime-factorization, forced-propagation: factoring out all $2$s and $3$s reveals the core that each condition preserves, and the status of each core propagates through its whole class.
